questions.question: What is component scanning in Spring Boot?
questions.title: Spring Boot component scanning explained
questions.direct_answer: Component scanning is Spring Boot's automatic bean discovery mechanism. At startup, Spring scans specified packages for classes annotated with @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller, and registers them as beans in the ApplicationContext. This eliminates manual bean configuration XML and enables dependency injection across your application.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands how Spring discovers and registers beans automatically without explicit XML or Java configuration.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Explaining component scanning as just 'finding classes' without mentioning bean registration or the ApplicationContext.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that @SpringBootApplication includes @ComponentScan by default, and explain the package scanning root.

sections.title: Component Scanning Fundamentals
sections.content: Component scanning is Spring's mechanism for **automatically discovering** and **registering beans** without writing explicit configuration. Think of it like airport security scanning for prohibited items—Spring scans your codebase looking for classes marked with stereotype annotations. When your Spring Boot application starts, the **component scanner** walks through specified packages, identifies classes with **@Component**, **@Service**, **@Repository**, or **@Controller**, and registers them in the **ApplicationContext** (Spring's IoC container). This is WHY you can inject dependencies without manually creating instances—Spring already created and registered those objects during startup. Without component scanning, you'd need XML files or @Bean methods for every single object, which becomes unmanageable in real applications with hundreds of services and repositories.

sections.title: Component Scanning in Action
Key Points
content: **@SpringBootApplication**: Combines @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, and @ComponentScan—you don't need to add @ComponentScan explicitly
**Stereotype annotations**: @Component is the generic marker; @Service, @Repository, @Controller are specialized versions that add semantic meaning
**Bean registration**: Component scanning creates singleton instances by default and stores them in the ApplicationContext with bean names derived from class names
**Package root**: Scanning starts from the package of the @SpringBootApplication class and includes all sub-packages recursively
**Classpath scanning**: Spring reads compiled .class files at runtime using reflection—no source code access needed
**Performance**: Component scanning happens once at startup; the cost is paid upfront, not during request handling
**Exclusion filters**: You can exclude specific classes or patterns from scanning using @ComponentScan(excludeFilters = ...) if needed

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Component scanning is Spring's way of automatically finding and registering beans without manual configuration. When your Spring Boot app starts, it scans packages looking for classes marked with annotations like at-Component, at-Service, at-Repository, or at-Controller. Once it finds them, Spring creates instances and puts them into the ApplicationContext, which is Spring's container that holds all managed objects. This is why you can use at-Autowired to inject dependencies—Spring already created those beans during the scan. The scanning starts from the package where your main class with at-SpringBootApplication lives, and it checks all sub-packages automatically. For example, if your main class is in com.bookstore, Spring will scan com.bookstore.service, com.bookstore.repository, and any other sub-packages. One thing to watch out for: if you put a service class in a sibling package like com.utilities, Spring won't find it because that's outside the scan root. You'd need to explicitly add that package using at-ComponentScan. The big advantage here is you don't write XML configuration files or dozens of at-Bean methods—Spring handles the wiring automatically.

speakable_v2.hook: Component scanning is how Spring finds your classes without you listing every single bean manually.

beats.text: When Spring Boot starts, it scans the package that contains your main @SpringBootApplication class — and all sub-packages below it. Any class annotated with @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller, or @RestController gets detected and registered as a bean in the ApplicationContext. That bean is then available for @Autowired injection everywhere else.

Without component scanning you'd have to register every bean manually in a @Configuration class — a line per class, every time you add one. In a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application with dozens of services and repositories, component scanning eliminates all that boilerplate. The @ComponentScan part of @SpringBootApplication is what makes this work automatically.

questions.question: What is the difference between @Component, @Service, @Repository, and @Controller?
questions.title: @Component vs @Service vs @Repository vs @Controller
questions.direct_answer: All four annotations register a class as a Spring bean through component scanning. @Service, @Repository, and @Controller are specializations of @Component. The key difference: @Repository adds automatic exception translation from SQL exceptions to Spring's DataAccessException. @Controller integrates with Spring MVC for web handling. @Service is purely semantic with no extra behavior.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows these are all bean registration annotations but understands the functional difference in @Repository exception translation.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying they're 'just for documentation' without knowing @Repository adds exception translation and @Controller has MVC integration.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @Repository, @Service, @Controller are meta-annotated with @Component, and give a concrete example of DataAccessException translation.

sections.title: Understanding Stereotype Annotations
sections.content: These four annotations solve the same core problem: registering a class as a Spring bean. **@Component** is the generic stereotype — you can use it on any class you want Spring to manage. The other three — **@Service**, **@Repository**, and **@Controller** — are specialized versions that inherit from @Component (they're meta-annotated with it). Spring treats them all as component scan targets. The difference is semantic clarity and added functionality. **@Repository** adds Spring's persistence exception translation, converting database-specific exceptions into Spring's unified **DataAccessException** hierarchy. **@Controller** marks a class as a Spring MVC web controller and enables request mapping. **@Service** has no extra behavior — it's purely a semantic marker for business logic classes.

sections.title: When to Use Each Annotation
sections.content: Use **@Repository** on DAO or repository classes that interact with databases. The exception translation is valuable — if your JPA or JDBC code throws a SQLException, Spring wraps it in a DataAccessException, making your code database-agnostic. Use **@Service** on classes that contain business logic — calculations, validations, orchestration between repositories. Even though it doesn't add functionality, it documents your architecture clearly. Use **@Controller** or **@RestController** on web layer classes that handle HTTP requests. Spring MVC looks for these to wire up endpoints. Use **@Component** when none of the specialized annotations fit — utilities, factories, or cross-cutting concerns like event listeners.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Meta-annotation**: @Service, @Repository, @Controller are all meta-annotated with @Component, so they inherit its bean registration behavior
**Exception translation**: @Repository is the only one with extra functionality, wrapping database exceptions in DataAccessException
**Semantic clarity**: using the right annotation documents your architecture and makes code easier to understand
**Component scanning**: all four are detected during classpath scanning, no functional difference in discovery
**Spring MVC**: @Controller enables request mapping and view resolution, but @RestController (which extends it) is more common in REST APIs
**No enforcement**: Spring doesn't validate you used the 'right' annotation, but following conventions helps maintainability
**Bean name**: by default, the bean name is the class name with lowercase first letter, same for all stereotypes

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: All four annotations register a class as a Spring bean, so they all work with component scanning and dependency injection. The difference is what layer they're meant for and whether they add extra functionality. At-Component is the generic one — you can use it on any class. At-Service, at-Repository, and at-Controller are specialized versions that are actually meta-annotated with at-Component under the hood. At-Service is used for business logic classes. It doesn't add any special behavior, it's just a semantic marker that tells other developers this class handles business rules. At-Repository is for data access classes like JPA repositories or JDBC DAOs. This one actually does something extra — it enables Spring's exception translation. If your database code throws a SQLException, Spring wraps it in a DataAccessException, which is part of Spring's own exception hierarchy. That way your code isn't coupled to a specific database technology. At-Controller is for the web layer. It tells Spring MVC this class handles HTTP requests. In REST APIs, you'd usually use at-RestController instead, which combines at-Controller with at-ResponseBody. A common mistake is thinking these are just for documentation, but at-Repository's exception translation is a real functional difference. Use the right annotation for the right layer and your code will be clearer and more maintainable.

speakable_v2.hook: All four register a bean — but @Repository does something extra that the others don't.

beats.text: From Spring's perspective, @Service, @Repository, and @Controller are all just @Component with a label. All four get detected by component scan and registered as beans. The difference is what each annotation adds on top of that.

rows: Exception translation: SQL errors become DataAccessException

beats.text: @Repository's exception translation is the one functional difference worth remembering. In a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application it means your service layer only catches Spring's DataAccessException, not raw Hibernate or JDBC exceptions. @Service is purely documentation — it tells other developers this is the business logic layer.

questions.question: What is the default component scan base package in Spring Boot?
questions.title: Default component scan package in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: The default scan base is the package containing the @SpringBootApplication class, plus all its sub-packages. If your main class is in com.example.bookstore, Spring scans com.example.bookstore.service, com.example.bookstore.repository, etc., but NOT sibling packages like com.example.utils. This is why 'bean not found' errors happen when components are outside the main package tree.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the component scan root and can troubleshoot common 'bean not found' issues caused by package structure.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking Spring scans the entire project or all com.example packages, not realizing it's anchored to the main class package.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @SpringBootApplication includes @ComponentScan, and mention how to override the base packages if needed.

sections.title: Default Component Scan Package Root
sections.content: Spring Boot's component scanning isn't project-wide—it's **anchored to a specific starting point**. The default base package is determined by the location of your **@SpringBootApplication** class. If your main class is com.bookstore.BookstoreApplication, Spring scans com.bookstore and every package underneath it (com.bookstore.service, com.bookstore.repository.impl, etc.). Think of it like a file system search starting from a root directory—it explores all subdirectories but doesn't backtrack to parent or sibling directories. This design prevents Spring from accidentally scanning third-party libraries or unrelated modules in your project. The most common fresher mistake is putting a @Service class in com.utilities when the main class is in com.bookstore.app, then wondering why Spring throws **NoSuchBeanDefinitionException**. Understanding this root behavior helps you structure packages correctly from day one.

sections.title: Package Structure and Scan Behavior
Key Points
content: **Anchor point**: The package of the @SpringBootApplication class is the scan root—everything starts there
**Hierarchical scanning**: All sub-packages are included recursively; com.bookstore includes com.bookstore.service.impl.legacy
**Sibling exclusion**: Packages at the same level or above the main class package are NOT scanned by default
**Common error**: NoSuchBeanDefinitionException often means the bean class is outside the scan path—check package structure first
**Multi-module projects**: In Maven/Gradle multi-module setups, each module's scan root is independent unless explicitly configured
**Convention over configuration**: Spring Boot assumes you follow the convention of keeping the main class at the root of your application packages
**Debugging tip**: Enable debug logging for org.springframework.context.annotation to see exactly which packages and classes Spring scans

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The default base package for component scanning is the package where your main application class lives—the one with at-SpringBootApplication. If your main class is in com.bookstore, Spring will scan that package and everything underneath it. So com.bookstore.service, com.bookstore.repository, com.bookstore.controller.api—all those get scanned. But here's the key: Spring doesn't scan sibling packages or parent packages. If you have a class in com.utilities, that's not under com.bookstore, so Spring won't find it. This is actually a really common mistake freshers make when they're organizing code. You'll put a service in a separate utility package and then get a bean not found error when you try to autowire it. The fix is either move that class into the com.bookstore tree, or explicitly tell Spring to scan additional packages using at-ComponentScan with basePackages. The reason Spring works this way is to avoid scanning your entire project, including third-party libraries, which would slow down startup and potentially register beans you don't want.

speakable_v2.hook: Your main class placement determines what Spring scans — get it wrong and beans silently disappear.

beats.text: Spring Boot scans the package that contains your @SpringBootApplication class and everything below it in the package hierarchy. If your main class is in com.example.myapp, Spring scans com.example.myapp.service, com.example.myapp.repository, and so on. But it does NOT scan com.example.util — that's a sibling package, not a sub-package.

This is the cause of many 'No qualifying bean of type' errors in Spring Boot 3.2 REST API applications. Someone creates a utility class in a package that isn't under the main class, and Spring doesn't find it. The convention is to put the main class in the root package of your project — not inside a sub-package. Then everything else lives in sub-packages below it and gets scanned automatically.

questions.question: How do you configure component scanning to include additional packages?
questions.title: Configuring @ComponentScan base packages
questions.direct_answer: Use @ComponentScan(basePackages = {"com.example.myapp", "com.other.util"}) on your @SpringBootApplication class to add packages outside the default scan path. Alternatively, use @ComponentScan(basePackageClasses = {MyMarker.class, UtilMarker.class}) to reference marker classes whose packages should be scanned. This is type-safe and refactoring-friendly.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows how to configure Spring when the default package structure doesn't fit the project needs.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing about @ComponentScan at all, or suggesting moving all code into one package instead of configuring the scan.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention basePackageClasses as the type-safe alternative to string-based basePackages configuration.

sections.title: Configuring Additional Scan Packages
sections.content: Sometimes your application needs beans from packages outside the default scan root—maybe you're integrating a shared utilities module or a legacy codebase with a different package structure. Spring provides **@ComponentScan** to override or extend the default scanning behavior. You can specify additional packages using **basePackages** (string-based paths) or **basePackageClasses** (referencing actual classes). The basePackageClasses approach is **type-safe**: if you refactor package names, the compiler catches the change, whereas string-based paths can break silently. This configuration goes directly on your @SpringBootApplication class. WHY does this matter? In multi-module Maven/Gradle projects, you often have shared libraries in different package hierarchies. Without explicit configuration, Spring won't discover those beans, leading to injection failures. Understanding both approaches helps you choose the right one for your project's maintainability needs.

sections.title: Configuring Additional Packages
Key Points
content: **basePackages attribute**: Accepts a string array of package names to scan; simple but vulnerable to refactoring errors
**basePackageClasses attribute**: Accepts class references; Spring scans the packages containing those classes—refactoring-safe
**Marker classes**: Common pattern is to create empty package-level classes (like PackageMarker.java) solely as scan targets
**Overriding default**: When you specify @ComponentScan explicitly, you must include the default package if you still want it scanned
**Multiple annotations**: You can use multiple @ComponentScan annotations (or @ComponentScans wrapper) for complex scenarios
**Filters**: @ComponentScan supports includeFilters and excludeFilters to fine-tune which classes get registered as beans
**Performance consideration**: Scanning additional large packages increases startup time—only add what you actually need

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: If you need Spring to scan packages outside the default root, you add at-ComponentScan to your main application class. There are two ways to do this. The first is basePackages, where you pass an array of package names as strings. For example, at-ComponentScan with basePackages equals open brace quote com.bookstore quote, quote com.shared.utils quote close brace. That tells Spring to scan both packages. The second way is basePackageClasses, which is more type-safe. Instead of strings, you reference actual classes from those packages. Spring then scans the package containing each class. So you'd write basePackageClasses equals open brace BookstoreApplication.class, UtilsMarker.class close brace. The advantage here is if you refactor and rename packages, your IDE updates the class references automatically, but string paths would break silently. One thing to remember: when you add at-ComponentScan explicitly, you're replacing the default behavior, so you need to include your main package too. If you only list com.shared.utils, Spring won't scan your com.bookstore packages anymore. This is useful in multi-module projects where you have shared libraries or when integrating legacy code that doesn't follow your package conventions.

speakable_v2.hook: When components live outside the default scan path, you override @ComponentScan — but there's a trap worth knowing.

beats.text: Add @ComponentScan to your @SpringBootApplication class with a basePackages array listing all packages you want scanned. But here's the trap: once you set basePackages explicitly, the default package (your main class's package) is no longer included automatically. You must add it to the list yourself, or your own beans won't be found.

A better approach for refactoring safety is basePackageClasses. Instead of string package names, you reference an actual class from each package. Spring derives the package from that class. If you rename the package, the refactoring tool updates the class reference too — unlike string literals which silently break. In a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application that shares components with other modules, basePackageClasses is the safer choice.

questions.question: What is the difference between @Component and @Bean?
questions.title: @Component vs @Bean in Spring
questions.direct_answer: @Component is a class-level annotation that marks your own classes for automatic detection during component scanning. @Bean is a method-level annotation in @Configuration classes where you write a factory method that produces and returns a bean instance. Use @Component for your code; use @Bean for third-party classes you can't annotate, or when you need complex instantiation logic.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands Spring's two distinct bean registration mechanisms and when to use each.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing the two or not realizing @Bean gives you programmatic control over instantiation and configuration.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @Bean methods can accept parameters (dependencies) and return any type, while @Component only works on classes you own.

sections.title: Two Paths to Bean Registration
sections.content: Spring offers two fundamentally different ways to register beans: **@Component** (and its specializations) and **@Bean**. **@Component** is for your own classes — you annotate the class itself, and Spring's component scanner finds it and registers an instance automatically. You don't write instantiation code. **@Bean** is for when you need explicit control. You write a method in a **@Configuration** class that creates and configures the object, then returns it. Spring calls your method and registers the returned object as a bean. WHY two mechanisms: @Component is simpler and works great for straightforward classes you own. But what if you need to create a third-party library object that you can't annotate? Or you need to conditionally configure a bean based on properties? Or instantiation requires multiple steps? That's when @Bean shines — you have full programmatic control. @Bean methods can accept parameters (dependencies Spring injects), perform logic, and return any type.

sections.title: When to Use Each Annotation
sections.content: Use **@Component** (or @Service, @Repository, @Controller) for your application classes — services, repositories, controllers, utilities. These are classes you wrote and can annotate. Component scanning handles everything automatically. The code is clean and declarative. Use **@Bean** when you need to register third-party classes that you can't modify to add @Component — like ObjectMapper from Jackson, RestTemplate from Spring, or DataSource from a JDBC driver. Also use @Bean when instantiation requires configuration logic: reading properties, calling builder methods, performing validation, or conditionally creating different implementations based on environment. @Bean methods in @Configuration classes give you a programmatic hook into the bean creation process.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **@Component**: class-level stereotype annotation for your own classes, requires component scanning to be detected
**@Bean**: method-level annotation in @Configuration classes, you write the factory method that returns the bean
**Third-party classes**: @Bean is the only way to register classes from libraries you don't control
**Instantiation control**: @Bean methods can contain logic, call builders, read properties, or perform validation
**Method parameters**: @Bean methods can declare dependencies as parameters, Spring injects them automatically
**Return type**: the method's return type becomes the bean type, can be an interface or abstract class
**Bean name**: defaults to method name for @Bean, class name with lowercase first letter for @Component

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: At-Component and at-Bean are two different ways to register beans in Spring, and they're used in different situations. At-Component is a class-level annotation you put on your own classes. When you mark a class with at-Component, or one of its specializations like at-Service or at-Repository, Spring's component scanner finds it automatically and creates an instance. You don't have to write any instantiation code, Spring handles it. This works great for your application classes like services, repositories, and controllers. At-Bean is a method-level annotation you use in a at-Configuration class. You write a method that creates and returns the object you want to register as a bean. Spring calls your method and registers whatever you return. This gives you full control over how the object is created. You'd use at-Bean in a few situations. First, when you need to register a third-party class that you can't annotate, like ObjectMapper from the Jackson library or RestTemplate from Spring itself. You can't go into those classes and add at-Component, so you write a at-Bean method instead. Second, when instantiation is complex and requires logic, like calling a builder, reading configuration properties, or choosing different implementations based on the environment. At-Bean methods can even accept parameters, and Spring injects those dependencies automatically. So in summary, use at-Component for your own classes when simple instantiation is enough. Use at-Bean for third-party classes or when you need programmatic control over bean creation.

speakable_v2.hook: @Component and @Bean both register beans — but they solve different problems and you need to know which to reach for.

beats.text: @Component is a class-level annotation for classes you own. Spring finds it via component scan and calls the constructor itself. @Bean is a method-level annotation in a @Configuration class — you write the factory method, you control how the object is created, and Spring registers whatever the method returns as a bean.

The practical rule: use @Component (or @Service, @Repository) for your own classes. Use @Bean for third-party classes you can't annotate — like RestTemplate, ObjectMapper, or a database connection pool. In a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application you'd typically configure RestTemplate or a WebClient in a @Configuration class with @Bean methods, while your services and repositories get @Service and @Repository.

questions.question: What is bean scope in Spring and what are the common scopes?
questions.title: Spring bean scopes — singleton vs prototype
questions.direct_answer: Bean scope controls the lifecycle and number of instances Spring creates. Singleton (default) means one shared instance per ApplicationContext. Prototype means a new instance every time the bean is requested. Web scopes include request (one per HTTP request) and session (one per HTTP session). Most application beans are singleton because they're stateless services or repositories.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands that singleton is the default, what it means, and when you'd need a different scope.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Spring singleton with the Gang of Four singleton pattern, or not realizing most beans are shared instances.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the thread-safety implication of singleton scope and why stateless design matters for shared beans.

sections.title: Understanding Bean Scope
sections.content: Bean scope defines the **lifecycle** and **number of instances** Spring creates for a bean. The default scope is **singleton**, which means Spring creates exactly one instance per ApplicationContext and shares it across all injection points. This is NOT the same as the Gang of Four Singleton pattern—Spring's singleton is per-container, not per-JVM. **Prototype** scope creates a new instance every time you request the bean. Web-specific scopes like **request** (one per HTTP request) and **session** (one per user session) tie the bean lifecycle to HTTP interactions. WHY does this matter? Singleton beans must be **thread-safe** because multiple threads handling concurrent requests share the same instance. If a singleton has mutable state (like instance variables you modify), you'll get race conditions. Most Spring beans (services, repositories, controllers) are naturally stateless, making singleton the right choice. Understanding scope prevents subtle concurrency bugs and helps you design thread-safe applications.

sections.title: Bean Scope Examples
Key Points
content: **Singleton scope**: Default scope; one instance per ApplicationContext; shared across all injection points; must be thread-safe
**Prototype scope**: New instance created every time the bean is injected or retrieved from the context; caller owns lifecycle
**Request scope**: One instance per HTTP request; automatically destroyed after response is sent; useful for request-specific data
**Session scope**: One instance per HTTP session; persists across multiple requests from the same user; typical for user preferences
**Thread-safety**: Singleton beans accessed by concurrent requests must not have mutable instance variables without synchronization
**Spring vs GoF singleton**: Spring singleton is per-container, not per-JVM; multiple ApplicationContexts can have separate instances
**Configuration**: Use @Scope annotation or XML scope attribute; common values are singleton, prototype, request, session, application

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Bean scope determines how many instances Spring creates and how long they live. The default is singleton scope, which means Spring creates one instance of the bean and reuses it everywhere. So if you have a UserService marked as at-Service, there's only one UserService object in memory, and every controller or component that injects it gets that same shared instance. This is different from the classic Singleton design pattern because it's one instance per Spring container, not per JVM. Then there's prototype scope, where Spring creates a brand new instance every time you ask for the bean. This is useful when the bean has mutable state, like a shopping cart—each user needs their own cart, not a shared one. For web applications, you also have request scope and session scope. Request scope creates one instance per HTTP request, so the bean lives only during that request's processing. Session scope creates one per user session, so it sticks around across multiple requests from the same user. The key thing to remember about singleton beans is they must be thread-safe because many threads will access them at the same time. That's why most Spring beans are designed to be stateless—they don't store changing data in instance variables. If you do have state, you need synchronization or you'll get concurrency bugs.

speakable_v2.hook: Singleton is the default scope — and it means all @Service beans are shared. That's why they must be stateless.

beats.text: Bean scope controls how many instances Spring creates for a given bean definition. The four scopes you need to know.

items: Singleton (default) — one instance per ApplicationContext. Every @Autowired injection gets the same object. Service and repository beans are almost always singleton.
Prototype — a new instance each time the bean is requested. Less common in practice.
Request — one instance per HTTP request. Useful for request-specific state.
Session — one instance per HTTP session. Useful for user-specific state across requests.

beats.text: The important implication of singleton scope: in a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application, your @Service beans are shared across all concurrent requests. If you store any mutable state in an instance field, concurrent requests corrupt each other's data. Singleton beans must be stateless — keep all request-specific data in local variables, not fields.

questions.question: What is @Autowired and how does Spring resolve which bean to inject?
questions.title: @Autowired and Spring dependency injection
questions.direct_answer: @Autowired tells Spring to inject a dependency automatically. Spring resolves it by type first: it looks for a bean whose type matches the field, parameter, or setter. If multiple beans of that type exist, Spring resolves by name (matching the field name to a bean name). Use @Qualifier("beanName") to explicitly specify which bean to inject when there's ambiguity.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands Spring's dependency injection resolution mechanism and can troubleshoot ambiguous injection scenarios.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing the by-type-then-by-name resolution order, or not understanding when @Qualifier is needed.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that constructor injection is preferred over field injection, and explain why (testability, immutability).

sections.title: Dependency Injection with @Autowired
sections.content: **@Autowired** is Spring's annotation for automatic dependency injection—it tells Spring to supply the required dependency instead of you manually creating instances. Spring uses a **two-phase resolution strategy**: first by **type** (matching the class/interface), then by **name** (matching the field or parameter name to a bean name). If you have one bean of type UserRepository, Spring injects it automatically. If you have two implementations of the same interface (PostgresUserRepository and MongoUserRepository), Spring needs additional help—either match the field name to a bean name (private UserRepository postgresUserRepository;) or use **@Qualifier** to specify explicitly. WHY this matters: constructor injection with @Autowired is the recommended approach because it makes dependencies explicit, enables immutability (final fields), and simplifies unit testing (you can pass mock objects without Spring). Field injection (private @Autowired UserService service;) is convenient but makes testing harder and hides dependencies.

sections.title: Autowiring and Disambiguation
Key Points
content: **Resolution order**: Spring matches by type first; if multiple candidates exist, it falls back to matching by name (field/parameter name to bean name)
**@Qualifier annotation**: Explicitly specifies which bean to inject when multiple beans of the same type exist; more reliable than name matching
**Constructor injection**: Preferred style because it enables immutable fields (final), makes dependencies explicit, and simplifies testing without Spring
**Field injection**: @Autowired on private fields is convenient but makes testing harder and hides dependencies; avoid in production code
**Setter injection**: @Autowired on setter methods allows optional dependencies; useful when the dependency might not always be available
**required attribute**: @Autowired(required = false) allows injection to fail gracefully if no bean exists; bean will be null
**NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException**: Thrown when multiple beans match by type and Spring can't resolve by name; fix with @Qualifier or @Primary

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: At-Autowired tells Spring to automatically inject a dependency instead of you creating it with the new keyword. When Spring sees at-Autowired, it first tries to find a bean by type. So if you have a field of type UserRepository, Spring looks in the ApplicationContext for a bean of that type and injects it. If there's only one, you're done. But if there are multiple beans of the same type—like maybe you have two UserRepository implementations for Postgres and Mongo—Spring needs to resolve the ambiguity. The second step is matching by name. If your field is named postgresUserRepository, Spring looks for a bean with that exact name. If the names match, it injects that bean. If they don't match, Spring throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException. The cleaner way to handle this is using at-Qualifier. You add at-Qualifier with the bean name in quotes right next to at-Autowired, and Spring knows exactly which bean you want. One important thing: constructor injection is better than field injection. With constructor injection, you make your dependencies final, which means they can't be changed after creation. It also makes your class easier to test because you can pass in mock objects without needing Spring. Field injection is tempting because it's less code, but it makes testing harder and hides what your class actually depends on.

speakable_v2.hook: @Autowired resolves by type — but when there are multiple candidates, you need to know how to break the tie.

beats.heading: Resolution order
beats.text: @Autowired tells Spring to inject a bean. Spring resolves it by type first — it finds all beans of the matching type. If there's exactly one, it injects it. If there are multiple, it tries to match by field name. If that still doesn't work, it throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException. Fix: add @Qualifier with the specific bean name, or mark one implementation with @Primary to set a default.

beats.heading: Constructor vs field injection
beats.text: In a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application, prefer constructor injection over field injection. With constructor injection, dependencies are declared explicitly as constructor parameters, can be marked final, and the class is fully testable with plain Java without a Spring context. Spring 4.3+ injects single-constructor beans automatically — no @Autowired annotation needed on the constructor.
